## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

# List available commands
default:
    @just --list

# Install Cargo tools required for local development
install-tools:
    cargo install cargo-nextest --locked
    cargo install cargo-llvm-cov --locked
    cargo install cargo-machete --locked
    cargo install cargo-mutants --locked
    cargo install cargo-semver-checks --locked
    rustup component add llvm-tools-preview

# Check the public Rust API of every published library crate for SemVer breaks against the last published version.
# The version only moves in the release PR, so a break is accepted when a pending minor or major changeset covers the
# crate. The CLI crate is a binary and has no library API.
semver:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -uo pipefail
    status=0
    for crate in caliper-docgen-core caliper-docgen-semantic caliper-docgen-tsc-client; do
        if cargo semver-checks check-release -p "$crate"; then
            continue
        fi
        if grep -qsE "^cargo/$crate: (minor|major)$" .changeset/*.md; then
            echo "breaking API changes are covered by a pending minor or major changeset for $crate"
            continue
        fi
        echo "breaking API changes need a minor or major changeset for cargo/$crate" >&2
        status=1
    done
    exit "$status"

# Build with the minimum supported Rust version declared in Cargo.toml.
msrv:
    cargo +$(sed -n 's/^rust-version = "\(.*\)"/\1/p' Cargo.toml) check --workspace --exclude caliper-docgen-napi --locked

# Install all dependencies
install:
    pnpm install
    cargo fetch

# Build all projects. Rust crates build via one workspace-wide cargo
# invocation, not `moon run :build` — that fans out one `cargo build -p`
# per crate, and every one of those processes contends for the same
# target/ file lock, serializing what moon's own scheduler thinks is
# parallel work (confirmed via `Blocking waiting for file lock` in verbose
# output). napi/vite-plugin have no such lock to contend over, so moon
# still orchestrates those directly.
build:
    cargo build --workspace --exclude caliper-docgen-napi
    moon run napi:build vite-plugin:build
    cargo build --release

# Run all tests (Rust, the native binding crate, TypeScript, Python)
test: test-rust test-napi test-ts test-py

# Run Rust tests (via nextest, which doesn't run doctests — paired
# with `cargo test --doc` to cover those too)
test-rust:
    cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude caliper-docgen-napi --locked
    cargo test --doc --workspace --exclude caliper-docgen-napi

# The binding crate is excluded from the workspace recipes, so its own unit tests run here.
test-napi:
    cargo nextest run -p caliper-docgen-napi --locked

# Run the Python tests for the weekly and agent-eval scripts (standard library only, no dependencies)
test-py:
    python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_*.py'

# Run TypeScript tests
test-ts:
    pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-vite-plugin test
    pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-storybook test
    pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle test

# Compare the Go checker and tsrs on every construct-suite row (run on every tsrs bump; see apps/oracle/construct-suite/README.md)
test-parity:
    pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle construct:parity

# The checker gates of ADR 0026, with nothing allowed to skip: the golden check, tsrs-against-Go parity, and the construct
# suite through the checker path held to checker-expectations.json. The pinned tsrs binary is the one the `tsrs` package
# itself selects for this platform (@tsrs/<os>-<arch>[-gnu|-musl]); see apps/oracle/construct-suite/README.md.
test-checker-lane:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    cargo build --release --locked -p caliper-docgen
    export REQUIRE_TSRS=1 REQUIRE_CALIPER_BIN=1 CALIPER_BIN="$PWD/target/release/caliper-docgen"
    TSRS_BIN="$(pnpm --silent --filter caliper-docgen-oracle exec tsx src/tsrs-bin.ts)"
    export TSRS_BIN
    echo "tsrs: $TSRS_BIN"
    pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle construct:check
    pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle construct:parity
    CALIPER_SEMANTIC=1 pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle construct:checker
    pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle exec vitest run tests/construct-checker-lane.test.ts

# Build the native binding and run the Vite plugin against it
test-integration:
    pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-napi build:napi
    NAPI_BINARY_REQUIRED=true pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-vite-plugin test:integration
    NAPI_BINARY_REQUIRED=true pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-storybook test:integration

# Measure ADR 0026's memory and determinism gates against the pinned tsrs (docs/gate-measurements.md). Builds the large
# project outside the repository (GATE_FIXTURES, default ~/Projects/caliper-fixtures/gate-large), so it needs the network
# or a warm pnpm store; `just gate-measure --edits 650 --runs 3` passes options to the harness. Takes minutes.
gate-measure *args:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    fixtures="${GATE_FIXTURES:-$HOME/Projects/caliper-fixtures/gate-large}"
    node scripts/gate_fixtures.mjs "$fixtures"
    cargo build --release --locked -p caliper-docgen-semantic --example gate_harness
    TSRS_BIN="$(pnpm --silent --filter caliper-docgen-oracle exec tsx src/tsrs-bin.ts)"
    for gate in memory determinism; do
        target/release/examples/gate_harness "$gate" --src "$fixtures/src" --tsc "$TSRS_BIN" {{ args }}
    done

# The deterministic construct suite on the release binary: goldens current, then the suite, which must not skip
test-construct:
    cargo build --release -p caliper-docgen --locked
    CALIPER_BIN="$PWD/target/release/caliper-docgen" pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle construct:check
    CALIPER_BIN="$PWD/target/release/caliper-docgen" REQUIRE_CALIPER_BIN=1 pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle test

# Pack the npm packages and check napi arrives only as vite-plugin's transitive dependency (pm: npm or pnpm)
verify-install pm="pnpm":
    scripts/verify-install.sh {{ pm }}

# Run the criterion benchmarks (single fixtures); `just bench` compares a whole library against main
bench-criterion:
    cargo bench --workspace --exclude caliper-docgen-napi

# Rust and TypeScript line coverage; with a threshold, fails if either is below it
coverage threshold="": (coverage-rust threshold) (coverage-ts threshold)

# Rust coverage: writes lcov.info and prints the summary before enforcing the threshold
coverage-rust threshold="":
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    cargo llvm-cov nextest --workspace --exclude caliper-docgen-napi --locked --lcov --output-path lcov.info
    cargo llvm-cov report --summary-only
    if [[ -n "{{ threshold }}" ]]; then
      cargo llvm-cov report --summary-only --fail-under-lines "{{ threshold }}"
    fi

# TypeScript coverage: prints the summaries and writes each package's coverage/lcov.info
coverage-ts threshold="":
    pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-vite-plugin exec vitest run --coverage {{ if threshold != "" { "--coverage.thresholds.lines=" + threshold } else { "" } }}
    pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-storybook exec vitest run --coverage {{ if threshold != "" { "--coverage.thresholds.lines=" + threshold } else { "" } }}

## Layout

```
construct-suite/
  tsconfig.json              the options the checker reads the fixtures with
  expectations.json          row id -> allowed verdicts (and the reason for each gap)
  <family>/<NN>-<slug>.tsx   a fixture
  <family>/<NN>-<slug>.golden.json   its committed golden, written by construct:capture
```

A row id is `<family>/<NN>-<slug>`. The harness is `../src/construct-suite.ts` (pure helpers), `../src/construct-capture.ts` (the capture script) and `../tests/construct-suite.test.ts`. `seed/` holds the three rows that prove the harness. The other families are `literals`, `objects`, `tuples-arrays`, `utility-mapped`, `generics` and `react`.

A fixture declares one `interface Props` with one prop `p`, and exports a component `Row` that takes it:

```tsx
interface Props {
  p: 'small' | 'large'
}

export function Row(props: Props) {
  return null
}
```

## Commands

```sh
# Write the golden files: the checker (typescript-beta, the independent arbiter) over all fixtures in one program.
pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle construct:capture

# Re-capture and fail on any difference from the committed goldens. Run it when the TypeScript pin changes.
pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle construct:check      # same as: construct:capture --check

# The suite itself, with the package tests.
pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle test
```

The test runs one `extract` over this directory with the weekly's canonical options (`--html-attributes full --include-unexported --load-dependencies --collapse-inherited-props none`, plus `--no-cache --quiet`) and compares prop `p` of each `Row` with its golden. The binary is `$CALIPER_BIN`, or `target/release/caliper-docgen`. Without one the suite skips with a message and the rest of the package tests still pass.

## Adding a row

1. Write `<family>/<NN>-<slug>.tsx` (two digits, lowercase slug).
2. `pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle construct:capture`, and read the new `.golden.json`: `text` must be the type you meant.

## What a verdict means

Verdicts come from `compare` in `../src/oracle-compare.ts`, the weekly oracle's own comparison.

- `identical`, `spelled`: green. Caliper and the checker state the same type (`spelled` is the same type written another way, such as `'a' | string`).
- `less precise`, `wrong`, `missing`: Caliper's type is looser, describes something else, or the prop is not listed.
- `opaque with marker`: less precise, and Caliper said so (`degradedBy` on the prop). A marked type is honest; an unmarked `less precise` is a silent loss. A `wrong` type stays `wrong` with a marker.
- `checker any/error`: the golden itself has no type. That is a broken fixture, not a result.

A row is green or a documented gap. A gap lists the verdicts it may have, none of them green, and a `gap` reason. The test fails when a row moves either way: worse is a regression; better means the gap closed, so update the expectation (to green, dropping `gap`). A gap never allows `identical` or `spelled`, so an improvement cannot pass unnoticed.

The suite needs Caliper's release binary. A CI job should build it before the package tests and point the test at it:

```sh
cargo build --release -p caliper-docgen

```

Without the build step the suite skips, which is green but covers nothing; a job that must run it should check that the binary exists first.

## tsrs parity

ADR 0026 makes the Go checker (`typescript-beta`) the type authority and lets tsrs, the Rust port, stand in for it only while it agrees. `construct:parity` is that agreement check: it runs the same one-program capture as `construct:capture` once with the Go checker and once with the exact `tsrs` version pinned in `apps/oracle/package.json`, normalizes both through `src/oracle-checker.ts`, and compares every row on four facts: the normalized type, the `typeToString` text, and the prop type's `flags` and `intrinsicName` (the facts Caliper reads through the API to tell the error type from `any`). The weekly oracle keeps the Go checker as the independent arbiter; this run does not replace it.

A reported difference is a row where tsrs gives a different answer than the Go checker. The report names the row, both `typeToString` texts, the differing facts, and a diff of the two normalized forms (`-` Go, `+` tsrs). Treat it as a tsrs bug or a protocol change until shown otherwise: do not pin that tsrs version, and report it upstream.

`parity-allowlist.json` maps a row id to the reason its difference is harmless (for example a lib file path inside an `import("...")` text). Add an entry only for a difference that cannot change the type Caliper reports, and give the reason. An entry whose row stops differing, or names no row, fails the run, so the list stays honest: remove it. The list is empty while every row is identical.

`tests/construct-parity.test.ts` runs the same comparison in-process. It skips with a warning when `tsrs` is not installed; set `REQUIRE_TSRS=1` to fail instead.

ADR 0026's gate before the default flips: the suite through the checker path (`--experimental-semantic-types` with the pinned `tsrs`), held to `checker-expectations.json`, which has the shape of `expectations.json`. ```sh

Regenerate an entry by running `CALIPER_SEMANTIC=1 TSRS_BIN=<path> pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-oracle construct:checker` and reading the report.

205	    /// Feed `hasher` everything `==` compares, so equal props hash equal (`ResolutionContext::share`).
206	    pub(crate) fn structural_hash<H: std::hash::Hasher>(&self, hasher: &mut H) {
207	        use std::hash::Hash;
208	        self.name.hash(hasher);
209	        self.prop_type.structural_hash(hasher);
210	        self.required.hash(hasher);
211	        if let Some(default) = &self.default_value {
212	            default.value.hash(hasher);
213	            default.computed.hash(hasher);
214	        }
215	        self.description.hash(hasher);
216	        self.tags.hash(hasher);
217	        for parent in self.parent.iter().chain(&self.declarations) {
218	            parent.name.hash(hasher);
219	            parent.file_name.hash(hasher);
220	        }
221	    }

224	    pub(crate) fn with_default_value(&self, default_value: DefaultValue) -> ParsedProp {

# 0022. Ask a warm checker for the requested component

**Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-10-26

## Context

The TypeScript 7.1 backend (ADR 0006, 0007) checks the whole project in one run: 0.5 to 9.4 s and up to 972 MiB on Chakra. A Storybook session asks about one component per story, and confidence scores computed from Caliper's own signals cannot say which components are wrong (`scripts/confidence.py`: at a 10% component budget the warning rule catches 23% of missing props, a risk table 3%, a logistic model 6%). Asking the checker for exactly the requested component needs no prediction.

`tsc --api` builds its program from the root files it is given and loads what they import. A program rooted at one component's file costs far less than the project, and the process stays up between programs. `crates/semantic/examples/ondemand_bench.rs`, 50 random components per corpus, TypeScript 7.1.0-beta, Apple silicon:

| Corpus | First answer | Per component, 1 / 8 / 32 per request | Whole project | Checker peak, one at a time / whole project |
| --- | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| Mantine | 137 ms | 41 / 6.6 / 2.7 ms | 605 ms | 180 / 276 MiB |
| Chakra | 703 ms | 534 / 259 / 108 ms | 9,446 ms | 350 / 972 MiB |
| shadcn | 82 ms | 28 / 8.6 / 3.3 ms | 1,518 ms | 157 / 899 MiB |
| antd | 91 ms | 37 / 6.1 / 8.4 ms | 489 ms | 612 / 436 MiB |
| Spectrum | 131 ms | 21 / 6.5 / 2.2 ms | 618 ms | 218 / 377 MiB |

Of a 30 to 40 ms request, 20 to 33 ms builds the program and 2 to 11 ms answers the queries. Initializing the session and parsing the tsconfig once per process, instead of per request, took 10 ms off. For the same components the checker reports 893 props where the structural pass reports 387 on shadcn, 828 against 732 on antd, and the same count on Mantine, Chakra and Spectrum.

Through the Storybook harness (`storybook-parity.mjs --variants caliper,caliper-ondemand`, shadcn 95 and antd 83 sampled stories, two runs each, shared machine):

| Corpus | Variant    | First story | Median story |     Total |    Peak RSS | Props Storybook lists that we lack |
| ------ | ---------- | ----------: | -----------: | --------: | ----------: | ---------------------------------: |
| shadcn | structural |   75-144 ms |      2-10 ms | 0.4-1.9 s | 314-324 MiB |                                  0 |
| shadcn | on-demand  |  101-335 ms |     29-66 ms | 3.0-7.1 s | 318-328 MiB |                                  0 |
| antd   | structural |   59-102 ms |       2-4 ms | 0.2-0.5 s | 222-226 MiB |                                 37 |
| antd   | on-demand  |   96-147 ms |     39-53 ms | 3.3-4.6 s | 229-230 MiB |                                  2 |

Memory is the addon's; the checker's process is not in the harness figure. With the merge below, shadcn lists every prop Storybook does and antd lacks 2 (`ref`, which the policy omits, and the `capture` attribute, which the curated set does not carry). Default structural mode lacks 37 on antd: `ref`, `capture`, and PurePanel's own and DOM props.

## Decision

A session can have a checker attached (`WatchSession::with_semantic`, a `SemanticProvider` the semantic crate implements). Core owns the trait and the merge; the checker's process, protocol and threads stay in `caliper-docgen-semantic`, so core does no I/O.

- `component(key)` computes the structural answer, asks the checker for that component, and waits up to `semanticWaitMs` (default 150). An answer in time is merged by name: where both have a prop the checker's type, optionality and description win, defaults, tags, `parent` and `declarations` stay structural, and every structural prop the checker did not return stays as the structural pass resolved it. One `Info` provenance diagnostic says so and counts the props kept. A slower checker leaves the structural answer and one `Info` diagnostic saying so; its late answer is kept for the next request.
- `htmlAttributes` means the same in both engines, because the checker reports what `@types/react` declares (`children`, `aria-*`, handlers, `className`) flagged `reactDeclared`, never filtered on its side, and the session applies the policy once after the merge (`react_types::checker_prop_used`). `full` takes all of them. `curated` and `none` take only those the structural pass already lists among the component's props (`children` through `PropsWithChildren`, or declared by the component), so the curated attributes and the absence in `none` stay the structural pass's. The request asks only for those names (`SemanticTarget::react_wanted`), so a component does not convert hundreds of DOM attributes it would drop. `key` is omitted in every mode, the one constant that says so being `REACT_SPECIAL_PROPS` in `react_types.rs`. `ref` is a prop (React 19 passes it to function components): `curated` and `full` list it for `ComponentProps<"div">`-style props and for `forwardRef` components, and `none` only when the component declares it.
- Answers are cached in memory by component key and the content hash of its file. An edit is a new question.
- The checker runs on its own thread with its own runtime, so a caller on any thread can bound its wait. `tsc` starts in the background when the session is created. It is replaced after 64 programs (antd reached 612 MiB after 50) and after a crash; three crashes keep it down for the session.
- A missing or unpinned `tsc`, a crash or a timeout yields the structural answer and one `Warning` per session. A request never fails because of the checker.
- The option is `semanticTypes: 'off' | 'on-demand'` on the native session and the Storybook addon, with `tscPath` and `semanticWaitMs`. It is off by default and experimental, as ADR 0007 requires.

## Consequences

- A story gets the checker's props when the checker is warm and answers inside the wait: usually the first story on Mantine, shadcn, antd and Spectrum (82 to 137 ms), and later stories on those at 21 to 41 ms each. That is above the 5 to 20 ms a story can afford, so a story that is not cached takes the structural answer when the checker is busy. Chakra's 534 ms per component never fits the wait; its answer arrives for the next request.
- The gain is where the structural pass is behind: shadcn's props more than double. On Mantine, Chakra and Spectrum the checker adds nothing, and the mode only costs a process.
- Batching a request to 8 files costs 6 to 9 ms per component (Chakra 259), 32 files 2 to 8 ms (Chakra 108). A prefetch of the components a project's stories name would make most requests cache hits; it is not built here.
- The cache is in memory. Reading and writing it under `node_modules/.cache` across runs is the next step, keyed by file hash, tsconfig and lockfile hash, and TypeScript version.
- The pin to `7.1.0-beta` stays until TypeScript 7.1 is stable; a version range and a startup `--version` check replace it then.
- Peak memory is a `tsc` process of 157 to 612 MiB next to the session. The 64-program replacement bounds it; a memory cap by RSS is not built.

## Alternatives considered

- One program over the whole project, started in the background. It costs 0.5 to 9.4 s and 276 to 972 MiB, and a single `tsc` answers requests one at a time, so a story would queue behind it.
- Route only components a score marks risky. The score measured here catches too few of the components that are wrong (#208) to decide which to send.
- Run the checker in the Storybook process. `tsc` is a separate Go binary reached over a pipe; a thread and a runtime of our own keep the session `Send + Sync` without nesting runtimes.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Whole-project checker run on gate-large through the CLI: wall time, peak RSS, diagnostics about the checker.
# usage: whole.sh <caliper-bin> <tsrs> <out-prefix> [extra args]
set -uo pipefail
bin="$1"; tsrs="$2"; out="$3"; shift 3
cd "$HOME/Projects/caliper-fixtures/gate-large" || exit 1
/usr/bin/time -l "$bin" extract --src src --json --load-dependencies --collapse-inherited-props none --no-cache --quiet \

grep -E "real|maximum resident" "$out.time"
python3 -I -c "
import json,sys
d=json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))

for x in d['diagnostics']:
    if x.get('code')=='semanticBackend' or 'checker' in x.get('message',''):
        print(x.get('severity'), x['message'][:200])
" "$out.json"

lines: +/// ADR 0026 S4: how long a story waits for the checker's answer through the Rust client. Each run opens a fresh session
+/// as the addon does (the checker started in the background at creation), waits until that process is up, then asks for
+/// `key` once and times the whole answer: the structural pass and the checker's program and conversion for the
+/// component. Passes when every answer is the checker's and the median is at most `budget_ms`, the addon's default
+fn first_answer(src: &Utf8PathBuf, tsc: &str, key: &str, runs: usize, budget_ms: u128) -> bool {
+    let (mut start, mut first, mut structural, mut answered) = (Vec::new(), Vec::new(), Vec::new(), 0);
+        let (session, checker) = open(src, tsc, Vec::new(), None);
+        // Queued behind the warm-up, an empty request returns once the process is up and initialized.
+        let answer = session.component(key).expect("the key is a component");
+    let (start_ms, first_ms, structural_ms) = (median(&mut start), median(&mut first), median(&mut structural));
+    let ok = answered == first.len() && first_ms <= budget_ms;

content.content:
1	# Semantic backend (TypeScript 7)
2	
3	**Status:** slice 1 implemented as an experimental opt-in, off by default ([ADR 0006](adr/0006-semantic-backend-as-second-resolver.md), [ADR 0007](adr/0007-backend-discovers-components-and-compiles-in.md)): `extract --experimental-semantic-types` (see "Slice 1" below). Structural extraction stays the default and the fallback. Separately, TypeScript 7.1's checker runs as a test-only oracle for structural prop types (`scripts/weekly.py --oracle`, `docs/measurement.md`). **Last verified:** 2026-10-23 for slice 1 against `7.1.0-beta`; 2026-09-27 for the Cost measurements, each naming its nightly; 2026-10-22 for the API table against the `7.1.0-beta` package; 2026-10-23 for the fixture-corpus parity on `7.1.0-beta`.
4	
5	## Next step
6	
7	Slice 1 below covers function components by their export. Next, in order: set what `PropType` now carries (index signatures, `readonly`, a ref type's name; optional and rest parameters are done), per-prop `tags` and `parent`, class and generic components, `batchRequests` to cut round trips and watch-mode notifications. The NAPI binding already ships: a session asks a warm checker for the requested component (`semanticTypes: 'on-demand'`, ADR 0022). The client's open Lifecycle items in the Gates table still stand.
8	
9	Some props can't be resolved from the AST alone. An opt-in backend asks TypeScript's checker instead, using the algorithm react-docgen-typescript (RDT) uses, and merges the answer into the structural result. Structural extraction stays the default.
10	
11	## What the structural resolver can't do
12	
13	Component prop counts from `fixtures/` with `--html-attributes full`, against RDT. Root causes are from `docs/benchmarks.md`.
14	
15	| Gap | Example | Ours | RDT |
16	| --- | --- | --: | --: |
17	| Generics through alias chains | ariakit `Props<T, O> = O & Omit<ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T>, keyof O>` | 5 | 294 |
18	| Generics through alias chains | ark-ui `SelectRoot` | 36 | 314 |
19	| Conditional types | headlessui `PropsOf<TTag>` | 14 | 246 |
20	| Mapped types over a generic | base-ui `WithBaseUIEvent<T>` | 11 | 293 |
21	| Conditional type and indexed access | fluentui `Slot<Type, ...>` | 8 | 303 |
22	| `@emotion/styled` two-argument overload | storybook-emotion `Button` | 7 | 306 |
23	
24	In the 2026-07-25 baseline, 10 of 33 compared components account for 2,696 of 2,720 missing props. The other 24 are `ref` and `key`, which this tool omits by design (`MIGRATING.md`).
25	
26	## How it works
27	
28	```
29	OXC parse → structural resolver ──────────────┐
30	                                              ├→ merge → ExtractionOutput
31	tsc --api → semantic resolver (opt-in) ───────┘
32	```
33	
34	The structural result is complete on its own and returns first. The semantic pass reads each exported component from the checker and replaces the structural props where it finds one.
35	
36	### Merge rules (proposed)
37	
38	| Field | Source |
39	| --- | --- |
40	| Props present, `type`, `required` | Semantic |
41	| `parent`, `declarations` | Semantic. `declarations` lists every declaring interface, not just the first |
42	| `description`, `tags` | Semantic JSDoc, structural if empty |
43	| `defaultValue` | Structural. RDT reads defaults from the AST too |
44	| Components tsc doesn't surface (not exported) | Structural only |
45	| Degrade diagnostics of a resolved component | Dropped |
46	
47	### What gets dropped, and where
48	
49	| Dropped | Where | Status |
50	| --- | --- | --- |
51	| `children` without a description | RDT projection only. Canonical keeps it | Done |
52	| Ambient `.d.ts` components such as `PureComponent` | Merge step | Done |
53	| `key` | Not emitted, matching the structural path | Closed |
54	| `ref` | Emitted in `curated` and `full` for `ComponentProps<"div">`-style props and `forwardRef` components, matching the structural path | Closed |
55	| HTML and DOM attributes in curated and none mode | Semantic adapter, by declaring interface rather than by name | Open |
56	
57	### Delivery (proposed)
58	
59	The structural result returns immediately. The semantic result follows: the CLI waits for it behind an opt-in flag, and the NAPI binding exposes a second async call so the Vite plugin can patch when it resolves. Spawn `tsc` at the start of the run so it loads while extraction runs. Each result carries a content hash, and a stale one is dropped.
60	
61	## Slice 1 (experimental, off by default)
62	
63	`caliper-docgen extract --experimental-semantic-types [--tsc-path PATH]`, or `experimentalSemanticTypes` and `tscPath` in `docgen.config.ts`. `crates/semantic` spawns the project's `node_modules/typescript/bin/tsc --api` or `node_modules/tsrs/bin/tsrs --api` (see "Supported binaries"), builds one program over the files of the components the structural pass found, and asks for each exported function component its call signature's first parameter and that type's properties. The CLI then calls core's `merge_semantic`. Not wired into watch, `check`, `inspect` or the NAPI binding.
64	
65	- **Merge:** props present, `type` and `required` from the checker; `defaultValue`, `parent`, `declarations`, `tags`, inheritance layers and curated inherited props stay structural. The checker is asked for a prop's description only when the structural pass has none (65% of Mantine's requests otherwise). Props `@types/react` declares are excluded by declaring file. Identical merged props are shared, as in the structural result.
66	- **Output type:** no new `PropType` variant and no schema change. Primitives, literals, unions (with `boolean` collapsed and `undefined` dropped from optional props), arrays, tuples, inline objects of up to 16 fields and single-signature functions map onto existing variants; `ReactNode`, `ElementType`, `CSSProperties` and `ReactElement` map to their terminals; anything else (named interfaces, enums, generics, overloads, anything past depth 4) is `Named` with the checker's own text. Union members keep the checker's order, which is creation order, not source order.
67	- **Names:** a symbol's `name` from the checker is its escaped name: a name that starts with two underscores has a third (`__size` arrives as `___size`, TypeScript's `escapeLeadingUnderscores`, so that it cannot collide with internal names such as `__call`). `rpc.rs` removes it when the answer is read, so every name downstream is the one the source writes.
68	- **Error type:** a name the checker cannot resolve (an import that does not resolve, a name declared nowhere) is typed with its error type, which carries the flags of `any`. Only `Type.intrinsicName` tells it from a written `any`: `"error"` against `"any"`, and the error type has an id per site, so the `any` id says nothing. `rpc.rs` reads `intrinsicName`; `convert.rs` turns an `"error"` type into an `opaque` type with the reason `unresolvableImport` (its `specifier` is the name as the source writes it, since the checker does not say which module was behind it), so the prop has `degradedBy: ["unresolvableImport"]` and a written `any` stays `any` with none. No new diagnostic code.
69	- **Provenance:** `Info` diagnostics with code `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` whose `affects` lists the output keys: one for the components the checker resolved, one per fallback reason. A first-class per-component field would change the canonical JSON and needs a `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump (`crates/core/src/types/output.rs`).
70	- **Fallback:** a missing, unsupported-version, crashed or timed-out `tsc` gives the structural result plus one `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` warning, never an error. Per component, the structural result stands for: not exported, class or non-function, overloaded, no props parameter, `any`/`unknown`/generic/union props type, export not found by name (a display name such as `@mantine/core/Accordion` also tries its last segment), or a request the checker rejected. Each is listed with its reason.
71	- **Parameter markers:** the checker's parameter symbols carry no optional or rest flag (an optional parameter has the same flags and `checkFlags` as a required one), so `convert.rs` reads them from what the checker prints for the function type: `name?: T` is optional and its `undefined` is dropped from the type, as for an optional prop, `...name: T[]` is the rest parameter; the signature's `flags` (`HasRestParameter`, bit 1) say the last parameter is a rest parameter either way. A parameter whose type is written `T | undefined` stays required. The type is printed with `typeToString` flags `NoTruncation | InTypeAlias` (plus the checker's own defaults): an alias at the top (`type Handler = (value?: string) => void`) is printed as the parameter list it stands for, not as `Handler`, and nothing is cut short. A `this` parameter is printed but is not one of the signature's parameters, and an overload set or a function with properties is printed as an object type whose signatures are read in order. When the printed type still does not give one entry per parameter (a callable interface prints as its name whatever the flags), a parameter is never taken to be required: the type is `opaque` with reason `unsupportedExpression`, so the prop carries `degradedBy`.
72	- **Not carried:** index signatures, `readonly` and ref names (`PropType` has them since `SCHEMA_VERSION` 4; `convert.rs` doesn't set them), generic parameters of functions, per-prop `tags`, `parent`/`declarations` from the checker. Default exports match by `default` when no export has the component's name.
73	- **Tests:** `crates/semantic/tests/replay.rs` runs the backend against `replay-tsc`, which answers from a recording of the real `7.1.0-beta` (`tests/fixtures/recording.json`, refreshed by `cargo run -p caliper-docgen-semantic --example record_fixture -- <typescript package dir>`; the `markers` fixture project, for names and parameters, records to `tests/fixtures/markers.recording.json` with the fixture name as a second argument; the `errors` fixture records the error type); a request the recording lacks fails the test. Fallbacks (no `tsc`, unsupported version, bad path, crash, hang) are asserted as the structural output plus one warning. The CLI test asserts the default output has no `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` diagnostic.
74	
75	Measured on `7.1.0-beta`, `extract --json` (best of 2 to 3), flag on against off, plus the base commit's output compared byte for byte (identical apart from `durationMs` on all five corpora, with and without `--load-dependencies`). Peak RSS is the larger of the two processes; on Chakra Caliper is 117 MiB and `tsc` 945 MiB.
76	
77	| Corpus   | Components resolved by the checker |            Off |              On |
78	| -------- | ---------------------------------: | -------------: | --------------: |
79	| mantine  |                          332 / 344 |  47 ms, 82 MiB | 588 ms, 287 MiB |
80	| chakra   |                          598 / 598 |  38 ms, 68 MiB |  9.3 s, 975 MiB |
81	| shadcn   |                      1,693 / 1,884 |  48 ms, 81 MiB |  1.5 s, 874 MiB |
82	| antd     |                          206 / 248 |  36 ms, 69 MiB | 508 ms, 443 MiB |
83	| spectrum |                      1,153 / 1,356 | 71 ms, 118 MiB | 618 ms, 381 MiB |
84	
85	Chakra's time is `tsc` computing 470,000 shared props' types, not round trips. Before shared props were interned in the merge, Caliper itself held 7.4 GiB on Chakra.
86	
87	Against the oracle (`scripts/weekly.py --oracle`, flag on, `7.1.0-beta`), wrong verdicts fall to 0.0% on every corpus but antd (0.1%), but the identical-or-spelled share also falls: mantine 91.3% to 22.0%, chakra 100% to 16.4%, shadcn 85.2% to 52.3%, antd 91.9% to 82.3%, spectrum 83.2% to 28.3%. The oracle credits the structural result for keeping a type's name (`StyleProp<MantineSpacing>`); the checker's answer is expanded to its members and compared as "less precise". Keeping the alias name and arguments needs a `PropType` that carries them, which is an output change.
88	
89	### Supported binaries
90	
91	Two packages provide the `--api` server, and both are used through the same client; neither is the default checker (the flag stays opt-in).
92	
93	- **`typescript`** from 7.1 on (`7.1.0-beta`, rc and stable): `node_modules/typescript/bin/tsc`.
94	- **`tsrs`** (`oxc-project/tsrs`, a Rust port of the TypeScript 7 checker): `node_modules/tsrs/bin/tsrs`, a Node shim that starts the platform binary from `@tsrs/<platform>`. Traced on the wire against `0.23.0-ts7.1.0-beta`: the same method sequence and the same results as `typescript@7.1.0-beta` on three recordings, and identical canonical output on Chakra, rdt-compat and blueprint.
95	
96	**Discovery.** `--tsc-path` (or `tscPath`) wins and must exist. Otherwise the search walks up from the project root and takes the first `node_modules` that holds either binary; inside one `node_modules`, `typescript/bin/tsc` comes before `tsrs/bin/tsrs`, so an install that has both keeps using `typescript`. Pass `--tsc-path` to choose `tsrs` there. The platform binary (`node_modules/@tsrs/<platform>/tsrs`) can be given with `--tsc-path` too and starts without Node.
97	
98	**Version rule** (`crates/tsc-client/src/supervisor.rs`, list in `crates/semantic/src/lib.rs`, `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS`). The version is read from the `package.json` of the package that owns the binary: the parent of `bin` for `typescript/bin/tsc` and `tsrs/bin/tsrs`, the binary's own directory for `@tsrs/<platform>/tsrs`. An entry is an exact version or a `major.minor` series. A `tsrs` version reads `<tsrs version>-ts<typescript version>`; it is accepted only when it is listed exactly (today `0.23.0-ts7.1.0-beta`, the build that was traced) and its TypeScript part is also taken by a TypeScript entry (`7.1`). A new `tsrs` release is therefore refused until someone traces it and adds it, as for any other build.
99	
100	The protocol detail that matters for `tsrs` is unchanged from `typescript`: the client sends `createPrograms[].compilerOptions` (the Node client sends `options`; the server accepts both, and `crates/semantic/tests/replay.rs` pins the key). Set `TSRS_BIN` to a `tsrs` binary to run `crates/semantic/tests/tsrs_real.rs` against the real thing; without it the test returns at once.
101	
102	## On demand, per component (experimental, off by default)
103	
104	A long-lived session (the Storybook addon, the lazy `WatchSession`) can attach a warm checker instead of running the whole-project pass above: `semanticTypes: 'on-demand'` (ADR 0022). `caliper-docgen-semantic` keeps one `tsc --api` process on its own thread, builds a program rooted at only the requested component's file, and returns its props. `WatchSession::component` merges them into the structural answer by name (the checker's type wins, a structural prop the checker did not return stays, and `htmlAttributes` applies once after the merge, as in the structural pass) when they arrive within `semanticWaitMs` (default 150 ms); otherwise it returns the structural answer plus an `Info` diagnostic, and the checker's late answer serves the next request of the same component while no source file has changed. Any source-file change, including a file the component only imports, drops every checker answer, so the next request asks again; an answer still in flight at that moment is not kept. The component's `OpaqueType`, `MaxDepthExceeded` and `CircularReference` diagnostics are dropped when the checker's props replace the structural ones, except while a structural prop the checker did not return is still opaque: those diagnostics name the component, not the prop, so they stay until nothing they could be about is left. (The whole-project merge drops unreturned structural props, so it has no such case.)
105	
106	Measured with `crates/semantic/examples/ondemand_bench.rs` (50 random components, TypeScript 7.1.0-beta): the first answer takes 82 to 137 ms (Chakra 703 ms), a component asked for alone 21 to 41 ms (Chakra 534 ms), and 2 to 9 ms when asked for in batches of 8 to 32. Where the structural pass is behind (shadcn) the checker reports 2.3 times the props; where it is not (Mantine, Chakra, Spectrum) it reports the same count. The in-memory cache, the 64-program process replacement and the failure modes are in the ADR.
107	
108	Hardening of the on-demand checker (still experimental, off by default):
109	
110	- **Versions:** `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS` is the `7.1` series (`7.1.0-beta`, rc and stable releases), not one pinned build. A supervisor entry is an exact version or a `major.minor` series; `7.10.0` is not `7.1`. The protocol has no version handshake, so the `package.json` version plus the initialize call that follows the spawn are the check; a build that fails either gives the structural result and one warning. Moving past 7.1 means re-tracing the protocol.
111	- **Memory:** after every fourth request, once the reply is sent, the worker reads the `tsc` process's resident memory (`/proc`, else `ps`) and replaces the process past `OnDemandConfig::max_rss_mib` (768 MiB; single-component programs peak at 157 to 612). The bound is between requests: one request that needs more finishes first. The 64-program replacement stays.
112	- **Start and stop:** creating the checker and `warm_up` return at once, a missing `tsc` answers the first request with the structural result and one diagnostic, and dropping the checker waits at most `shutdown_wait` (5 s) for a request in progress before letting the worker finish alone.
113	- **Tests:** the two tests against the real checker (`crates/semantic/tests/on_demand.rs`) run on CI with `CALIPER_TEST_TSC` set to `apps/oracle`'s `typescript-beta`; on CI a missing variable fails them. Locally they skip.
114	- **Latency, re-measured** (`ondemand_bench`, 30 components, release build, `7.1.0-beta`): shadcn first answer 84 ms, median 21 ms, p90 37 ms; antd first 93 ms, median 36 ms, p90 40 ms. The memory check does not add to a story's wait.
115	
116	## The algorithm
117	
118	Mirrors RDT 2.4.0 (`lib/parser.js`). Method names are from the 7.1 client.
119	
120	1. `getSymbolOfSourceFile(file)`, then `getExportsOfModule`.
121	2. For each export, `getTypeOfSymbol`, then `getSignaturesOfType(Call)`. A component has a signature whose first parameter is named `props` or is the only parameter. For a class, use `Construct` signatures and read `props` from the instance type.
122	3. Props type: `getTypeOfSymbolAtLocation(param, param.valueDeclaration)`. Props: the type's apparent properties, plus each member's when it is a union.
123	4. Per prop, `type` is `typeToString(getBaseConstraintOfType(t) ?? t)` with default flags, so long types truncate as they do in RDT. `required` means the symbol lacks `Optional` and has no code default.
124	5. `parent` is the first declaration's parent when that is an interface or type alias. `declarations` is every declaration's parent.
125	6. `description` and `tags` come from `getDocumentationComment` and `getJsDocTags`.
126	
127	RDT also emits any exported symbol that has a JSDoc comment but no props. We don't. In the fixture corpus, 23 of the 26 entries only RDT emits are of this kind, such as enum members, type aliases and functions.
128	
129	### The converter (ADR 0026, slice S2)
130	
131	A prop's checker type becomes a `PropType` from structured answers only (`crates/semantic/src/convert.rs`): the type flags, a union's members (`getTypesOfType`), a reference's arguments, a tuple type's element flags (`getTargetOfType`), an object's signatures, properties and index signatures (one `batchRequests`), and an alias's symbol and arguments. `typeToString` is used for a name to display, and for two facts the API does not state: which parameter is optional and what a tuple element is labeled (`printed.rs` reads them from the printed type and refuses text that does not read to its end; a fact it cannot read is never replaced by a guess).
132	
133	- **Named boundary.** An interface or class declared under `node_modules` or in the TypeScript lib (`Date`, `Promise<T>`, `HTMLElement`), and an object type a dependency's alias names, stay `named` with their arguments. A function type is always expanded. The lib's utilities (`Partial`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`) are expanded: their result is the type. A dependency's union of literals is expanded, since its members are the values a control offers. React's `ReactNode`, `ElementType`, `CSSProperties` and `ReactElement` are recognized by where they are declared.
134	- **Caps.** Depth 5, 500 members at the top and 120 below it (a union, an intersection, a tuple's elements), and a budget of 100 properties at the top and 40 below it that counts only the members the project did not declare (inherited from a dependency or the lib, or with no declaration). A cut type is `truncated` with the limit (and, for a width, the total), which `degradedBy` reports. Every descent into the parts of a type (an object, union, intersection, array, tuple or template literal) passes one gate (`Converter::enter`) that checks, before anything is fetched, whether the type encloses itself or is too deep; the width is checked after it, where the type is known. A test has a prop for each cap.
135	- **Wide object types.** What the project declares is listed whole however wide: an interface of 150 own fields is never cut. Over the budget of members from outside the project, the rest stands as what it is named through, and the project's own members stay beside it. A utility wrapper (`Omit`, `Pick`, `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`) is kept as `named` with its arguments when what it applies to has a name of its own: a React DOM attribute type becomes `htmlAttributes` (recognized by the declaring file `/@types/react/` and the interface's name, with the element read from its type argument by the same table the structural path uses, `HTMLAnchorElement` is `a`; an element the table does not know is not guessed), and another dependency or lib type is a `named` layer. The checker keeps no `ComponentPropsWithoutRef`, only the `Omit<..., "ref">` it expands to, which is kept as written. Under the budget the wrapper is expanded (`Pick<ComponentProps<"button">, "disabled" | "type">` has two props). A class or interface of the project that extends such types (`interface BoxProps extends Omit<HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>, "color">`) is an intersection of its own fields and each base type (`getBaseTypes`), a base of the project seen through to its own bases; an instantiation of a generic one, as the type itself or as one base among others, states no bases in terms of its arguments, so the type is cut: its members from outside are `truncated` with their real count beside its own, and the other bases are not named in its place. A type that is not wrapped (`HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>` as a prop) is the `named` it always was.
136	- **React aliases flattened into a union.** The checker flattens `ReactNode | Fn` into the members of `ReactNode`, so a union that holds all of them (`ReactElement`, `ReactPortal` and an `Iterable` of `ReactNode`, found by declaration, with the primitives) is `reactNode` again beside the rest of its members. `ElementType` below the top of a prop arrives the same way and is wider than the budget: it is recognized (more than 100 of React's own tag names, a fixed table of `JSX.IntrinsicElements`, with `ComponentClass` and `FunctionComponent`) and kept as the terminal instead of cut, and only those tag names go into it: any other string literal the author wrote beside it (`ElementType | "custom-widget"`) stays a member of the union, as does a tag a project adds to `JSX.IntrinsicElements`; narrower, it is listed. `ReactElement`, `JSX.Element` and `ReactChild` stay collapsed to `reactNode` (ADR 0026).
137	- **Recursion** is a `recursive` marker named by the declaration (the alias or interface) with the instantiation's type arguments. Whether a type is one it is inside of is decided by its type handle, which is the instantiation: `Box<string>` inside `Box<Box<string>>` is another type from the one around it and is expanded, while `Tree<string>` inside `Tree<string>` is a back-reference; an alias of an array or tuple of itself (`type Loop = Loop[]`) ends at the first lap. A handle is only compared inside one conversion, never stored in an answer; type handles change with the order of queries, so a test asks last to first and compares bytes. The per-snapshot memo is keyed by the handle, the depth and the set of enclosing handles, so a hit gives what a miss would.
138	- **Union order.** The checker sorts a union's members by kind and value. Where the structural pass resolved the same union (in a parsed file, or a loaded dependency), the merge puts the members back in its order, which it read from the type node (`types/semantic/order.rs`). A union the structural pass left opaque keeps the checker's order, with no marker.
139	- **Debug stat.** With `RUST_LOG=caliper_docgen_semantic=debug`, each component logs its request count and milliseconds, and the session logs requests by method and memo hits.

# Semantic backend (TypeScript 7)

**Status:** slice 1 implemented as an experimental opt-in, off by default ([ADR 0006](adr/0006-semantic-backend-as-second-resolver.md), [ADR 0007](adr/0007-backend-discovers-components-and-compiles-in.md)): `extract --experimental-semantic-types` (see "Slice 1" below). Structural extraction stays the default and the fallback. Separately, TypeScript 7.1's checker runs as a test-only oracle for structural prop types (`scripts/weekly.py --oracle`, `docs/measurement.md`). **Last verified:** 2026-10-23 for slice 1 against `7.1.0-beta`; 2026-09-27 for the Cost measurements, each naming its nightly; 2026-10-22 for the API table against the `7.1.0-beta` package; 2026-10-23 for the fixture-corpus parity on `7.1.0-beta`.

## Next step

Slice 1 below covers function components by their export. Next, in order: set what `PropType` now carries (index signatures, `readonly`, a ref type's name; optional and rest parameters are done), per-prop `tags` and `parent`, class and generic components, `batchRequests` to cut round trips and watch-mode notifications. The NAPI binding already ships: a session asks a warm checker for the requested component (`semanticTypes: 'on-demand'`, ADR 0022). The client's open Lifecycle items in the Gates table still stand.

Some props can't be resolved from the AST alone. An opt-in backend asks TypeScript's checker instead, using the algorithm react-docgen-typescript (RDT) uses, and merges the answer into the structural result. Structural extraction stays the default.

## What the structural resolver can't do

Component prop counts from `fixtures/` with `--html-attributes full`, against RDT. Root causes are from `docs/benchmarks.md`.

| Gap | Example | Ours | RDT |
| --- | --- | --: | --: |
| Generics through alias chains | ariakit `Props<T, O> = O & Omit<ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T>, keyof O>` | 5 | 294 |
| Generics through alias chains | ark-ui `SelectRoot` | 36 | 314 |
| Conditional types | headlessui `PropsOf<TTag>` | 14 | 246 |
| Mapped types over a generic | base-ui `WithBaseUIEvent<T>` | 11 | 293 |
| Conditional type and indexed access | fluentui `Slot<Type, ...>` | 8 | 303 |
| `@emotion/styled` two-argument overload | storybook-emotion `Button` | 7 | 306 |

In the 2026-07-25 baseline, 10 of 33 compared components account for 2,696 of 2,720 missing props. The other 24 are `ref` and `key`, which this tool omits by design (`MIGRATING.md`).

## How it works

```
OXC parse → structural resolver ──────────────┐
                                              ├→ merge → ExtractionOutput
tsc --api → semantic resolver (opt-in) ───────┘
```

The structural result is complete on its own and returns first. The semantic pass reads each exported component from the checker and replaces the structural props where it finds one.

### Merge rules (proposed)

| Field | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Props present, `type`, `required` | Semantic |
| `parent`, `declarations` | Semantic. `declarations` lists every declaring interface, not just the first |
| `description`, `tags` | Semantic JSDoc, structural if empty |
| `defaultValue` | Structural. RDT reads defaults from the AST too |
| Components tsc doesn't surface (not exported) | Structural only |
| Degrade diagnostics of a resolved component | Dropped |

### What gets dropped, and where

| Dropped | Where | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `children` without a description | RDT projection only. Canonical keeps it | Done |
| Ambient `.d.ts` components such as `PureComponent` | Merge step | Done |
| `key` | Not emitted, matching the structural path | Closed |
| `ref` | Emitted in `curated` and `full` for `ComponentProps<"div">`-style props and `forwardRef` components, matching the structural path | Closed |
| HTML and DOM attributes in curated and none mode | Semantic adapter, by declaring interface rather than by name | Open |

### Delivery (proposed)

The structural result returns immediately. The semantic result follows: the CLI waits for it behind an opt-in flag, and the NAPI binding exposes a second async call so the Vite plugin can patch when it resolves. Spawn `tsc` at the start of the run so it loads while extraction runs. Each result carries a content hash, and a stale one is dropped.

## Slice 1 (experimental, off by default)

`caliper-docgen extract --experimental-semantic-types [--tsc-path PATH]`, or `experimentalSemanticTypes` and `tscPath` in `docgen.config.ts`. `crates/semantic` spawns the project's `node_modules/typescript/bin/tsc --api` or `node_modules/tsrs/bin/tsrs --api` (see "Supported binaries"), builds one program over the files of the components the structural pass found, and asks for each exported function component its call signature's first parameter and that type's properties. The CLI then calls core's `merge_semantic`. Not wired into watch, `check`, `inspect` or the NAPI binding.

- **Merge:** props present, `type` and `required` from the checker; `defaultValue`, `parent`, `declarations`, `tags`, inheritance layers and curated inherited props stay structural. The checker is asked for a prop's description only when the structural pass has none (65% of Mantine's requests otherwise). Props `@types/react` declares are excluded by declaring file. Identical merged props are shared, as in the structural result.
- **Output type:** no new `PropType` variant and no schema change. Primitives, literals, unions (with `boolean` collapsed and `undefined` dropped from optional props), arrays, tuples, inline objects of up to 16 fields and single-signature functions map onto existing variants; `ReactNode`, `ElementType`, `CSSProperties` and `ReactElement` map to their terminals; anything else (named interfaces, enums, generics, overloads, anything past depth 4) is `Named` with the checker's own text. Union members keep the checker's order, which is creation order, not source order.
- **Names:** a symbol's `name` from the checker is its escaped name: a name that starts with two underscores has a third (`__size` arrives as `___size`, TypeScript's `escapeLeadingUnderscores`, so that it cannot collide with internal names such as `__call`). `rpc.rs` removes it when the answer is read, so every name downstream is the one the source writes.
- **Error type:** a name the checker cannot resolve (an import that does not resolve, a name declared nowhere) is typed with its error type, which carries the flags of `any`. Only `Type.intrinsicName` tells it from a written `any`: `"error"` against `"any"`, and the error type has an id per site, so the `any` id says nothing. `rpc.rs` reads `intrinsicName`; `convert.rs` turns an `"error"` type into an `opaque` type with the reason `unresolvableImport` (its `specifier` is the name as the source writes it, since the checker does not say which module was behind it), so the prop has `degradedBy: ["unresolvableImport"]` and a written `any` stays `any` with none. No new diagnostic code.
- **Provenance:** `Info` diagnostics with code `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` whose `affects` lists the output keys: one for the components the checker resolved, one per fallback reason. A first-class per-component field would change the canonical JSON and needs a `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump (`crates/core/src/types/output.rs`).
- **Fallback:** a missing, unsupported-version, crashed or timed-out `tsc` gives the structural result plus one `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` warning, never an error. Per component, the structural result stands for: not exported, class or non-function, overloaded, no props parameter, `any`/`unknown`/generic/union props type, export not found by name (a display name such as `@mantine/core/Accordion` also tries its last segment), or a request the checker rejected. Each is listed with its reason.
- **Parameter markers:** the checker's parameter symbols carry no optional or rest flag (an optional parameter has the same flags and `checkFlags` as a required one), so `convert.rs` reads them from what the checker prints for the function type: `name?: T` is optional and its `undefined` is dropped from the type, as for an optional prop, `...name: T[]` is the rest parameter; the signature's `flags` (`HasRestParameter`, bit 1) say the last parameter is a rest parameter either way. A parameter whose type is written `T | undefined` stays required. The type is printed with `typeToString` flags `NoTruncation | InTypeAlias` (plus the checker's own defaults): an alias at the top (`type Handler = (value?: string) => void`) is printed as the parameter list it stands for, not as `Handler`, and nothing is cut short. A `this` parameter is printed but is not one of the signature's parameters, and an overload set or a function with properties is printed as an object type whose signatures are read in order. When the printed type still does not give one entry per parameter (a callable interface prints as its name whatever the flags), a parameter is never taken to be required: the type is `opaque` with reason `unsupportedExpression`, so the prop carries `degradedBy`.
- **Not carried:** index signatures, `readonly` and ref names (`PropType` has them since `SCHEMA_VERSION` 4; `convert.rs` doesn't set them), generic parameters of functions, per-prop `tags`, `parent`/`declarations` from the checker. Default exports match by `default` when no export has the component's name.
- **Tests:** `crates/semantic/tests/replay.rs` runs the backend against `replay-tsc`, which answers from a recording of the real `7.1.0-beta` (`tests/fixtures/recording.json`, refreshed by `cargo run -p caliper-docgen-semantic --example record_fixture -- <typescript package dir>`; the `markers` fixture project, for names and parameters, records to `tests/fixtures/markers.recording.json` with the fixture name as a second argument; the `errors` fixture records the error type); a request the recording lacks fails the test. Fallbacks (no `tsc`, unsupported version, bad path, crash, hang) are asserted as the structural output plus one warning. The CLI test asserts the default output has no `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` diagnostic.

Measured on `7.1.0-beta`, `extract --json` (best of 2 to 3), flag on against off, plus the base commit's output compared byte for byte (identical apart from `durationMs` on all five corpora, with and without `--load-dependencies`). Peak RSS is the larger of the two processes; on Chakra Caliper is 117 MiB and `tsc` 945 MiB.

| Corpus   | Components resolved by the checker |            Off |              On |
| -------- | ---------------------------------: | -------------: | --------------: |
| mantine  |                          332 / 344 |  47 ms, 82 MiB | 588 ms, 287 MiB |
| chakra   |                          598 / 598 |  38 ms, 68 MiB |  9.3 s, 975 MiB |
| shadcn   |                      1,693 / 1,884 |  48 ms, 81 MiB |  1.5 s, 874 MiB |
| antd     |                          206 / 248 |  36 ms, 69 MiB | 508 ms, 443 MiB |
| spectrum |                      1,153 / 1,356 | 71 ms, 118 MiB | 618 ms, 381 MiB |

Chakra's time is `tsc` computing 470,000 shared props' types, not round trips. Before shared props were interned in the merge, Caliper itself held 7.4 GiB on Chakra.

Against the oracle (`scripts/weekly.py --oracle`, flag on, `7.1.0-beta`), wrong verdicts fall to 0.0% on every corpus but antd (0.1%), but the identical-or-spelled share also falls: mantine 91.3% to 22.0%, chakra 100% to 16.4%, shadcn 85.2% to 52.3%, antd 91.9% to 82.3%, spectrum 83.2% to 28.3%. The oracle credits the structural result for keeping a type's name (`StyleProp<MantineSpacing>`); the checker's answer is expanded to its members and compared as "less precise". Keeping the alias name and arguments needs a `PropType` that carries them, which is an output change.

### Supported binaries

Two packages provide the `--api` server, and both are used through the same client; neither is the default checker (the flag stays opt-in).

- **`typescript`** from 7.1 on (`7.1.0-beta`, rc and stable): `node_modules/typescript/bin/tsc`.
- **`tsrs`** (`oxc-project/tsrs`, a Rust port of the TypeScript 7 checker): `node_modules/tsrs/bin/tsrs`, a Node shim that starts the platform binary from `@tsrs/<platform>`. Traced on the wire against `0.23.0-ts7.1.0-beta`: the same method sequence and the same results as `typescript@7.1.0-beta` on three recordings, and identical canonical output on Chakra, rdt-compat and blueprint.

**Discovery.** `--tsc-path` (or `tscPath`) wins and must exist. Otherwise the search walks up from the project root and takes the first `node_modules` that holds either binary; inside one `node_modules`, `typescript/bin/tsc` comes before `tsrs/bin/tsrs`, so an install that has both keeps using `typescript`. Pass `--tsc-path` to choose `tsrs` there. The platform binary (`node_modules/@tsrs/<platform>/tsrs`) can be given with `--tsc-path` too and starts without Node.

**Version rule** (`crates/tsc-client/src/supervisor.rs`, list in `crates/semantic/src/lib.rs`, `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS`). The version is read from the `package.json` of the package that owns the binary: the parent of `bin` for `typescript/bin/tsc` and `tsrs/bin/tsrs`, the binary's own directory for `@tsrs/<platform>/tsrs`. An entry is an exact version or a `major.minor` series. A `tsrs` version reads `<tsrs version>-ts<typescript version>`; it is accepted only when it is listed exactly (today `0.23.0-ts7.1.0-beta`, the build that was traced) and its TypeScript part is also taken by a TypeScript entry (`7.1`). A new `tsrs` release is therefore refused until someone traces it and adds it, as for any other build.

The protocol detail that matters for `tsrs` is unchanged from `typescript`: the client sends `createPrograms[].compilerOptions` (the Node client sends `options`; the server accepts both, and `crates/semantic/tests/replay.rs` pins the key). Set `TSRS_BIN` to a `tsrs` binary to run `crates/semantic/tests/tsrs_real.rs` against the real thing; without it the test returns at once.

## On demand, per component (experimental, off by default)

A long-lived session (the Storybook addon, the lazy `WatchSession`) can attach a warm checker instead of running the whole-project pass above: `semanticTypes: 'on-demand'` (ADR 0022). `caliper-docgen-semantic` keeps one `tsc --api` process on its own thread, builds a program rooted at only the requested component's file, and returns its props. `WatchSession::component` merges them into the structural answer by name (the checker's type wins, a structural prop the checker did not return stays, and `htmlAttributes` applies once after the merge, as in the structural pass) when they arrive within `semanticWaitMs` (default 150 ms); otherwise it returns the structural answer plus an `Info` diagnostic, and the checker's late answer serves the next request of the same component while no source file has changed. Any source-file change, including a file the component only imports, drops every checker answer, so the next request asks again; an answer still in flight at that moment is not kept. The component's `OpaqueType`, `MaxDepthExceeded` and `CircularReference` diagnostics are dropped when the checker's props replace the structural ones, except while a structural prop the checker did not return is still opaque: those diagnostics name the component, not the prop, so they stay until nothing they could be about is left. (The whole-project merge drops unreturned structural props, so it has no such case.)

Measured with `crates/semantic/examples/ondemand_bench.rs` (50 random components, TypeScript 7.1.0-beta): the first answer takes 82 to 137 ms (Chakra 703 ms), a component asked for alone 21 to 41 ms (Chakra 534 ms), and 2 to 9 ms when asked for in batches of 8 to 32. Where the structural pass is behind (shadcn) the checker reports 2.3 times the props; where it is not (Mantine, Chakra, Spectrum) it reports the same count. The in-memory cache, the 64-program process replacement and the failure modes are in the ADR.

Hardening of the on-demand checker (still experimental, off by default):

- **Versions:** `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS` is the `7.1` series (`7.1.0-beta`, rc and stable releases), not one pinned build. A supervisor entry is an exact version or a `major.minor` series; `7.10.0` is not `7.1`. The protocol has no version handshake, so the `package.json` version plus the initialize call that follows the spawn are the check; a build that fails either gives the structural result and one warning. Moving past 7.1 means re-tracing the protocol.
- **Memory:** after every fourth request, once the reply is sent, the worker reads the `tsc` process's resident memory (`/proc`, else `ps`) and replaces the process past `OnDemandConfig::max_rss_mib` (768 MiB; single-component programs peak at 157 to 612). The bound is between requests: one request that needs more finishes first. The 64-program replacement stays.
- **Start and stop:** creating the checker and `warm_up` return at once, a missing `tsc` answers the first request with the structural result and one diagnostic, and dropping the checker waits at most `shutdown_wait` (5 s) for a request in progress before letting the worker finish alone.
- **Tests:** the two tests against the real checker (`crates/semantic/tests/on_demand.rs`) run on CI with `CALIPER_TEST_TSC` set to `apps/oracle`'s `typescript-beta`; on CI a missing variable fails them. Locally they skip.
- **Latency, re-measured** (`ondemand_bench`, 30 components, release build, `7.1.0-beta`): shadcn first answer 84 ms, median 21 ms, p90 37 ms; antd first 93 ms, median 36 ms, p90 40 ms. The memory check does not add to a story's wait.

## The algorithm

Mirrors RDT 2.4.0 (`lib/parser.js`). Method names are from the 7.1 client.

1. `getSymbolOfSourceFile(file)`, then `getExportsOfModule`.
2. For each export, `getTypeOfSymbol`, then `getSignaturesOfType(Call)`. A component has a signature whose first parameter is named `props` or is the only parameter. For a class, use `Construct` signatures and read `props` from the instance type.
3. Props type: `getTypeOfSymbolAtLocation(param, param.valueDeclaration)`. Props: the type's apparent properties, plus each member's when it is a union.
4. Per prop, `type` is `typeToString(getBaseConstraintOfType(t) ?? t)` with default flags, so long types truncate as they do in RDT. `required` means the symbol lacks `Optional` and has no code default.
5. `parent` is the first declaration's parent when that is an interface or type alias. `declarations` is every declaration's parent.
6. `description` and `tags` come from `getDocumentationComment` and `getJsDocTags`.

RDT also emits any exported symbol that has a JSDoc comment but no props. We don't. In the fixture corpus, 23 of the 26 entries only RDT emits are of this kind, such as enum members, type aliases and functions.

### The converter (ADR 0026, slice S2)

A prop's checker type becomes a `PropType` from structured answers only (`crates/semantic/src/convert.rs`): the type flags, a union's members (`getTypesOfType`), a reference's arguments, a tuple type's element flags (`getTargetOfType`), an object's signatures, properties and index signatures (one `batchRequests`), and an alias's symbol and arguments. `typeToString` is used for a name to display, and for two facts the API does not state: which parameter is optional and what a tuple element is labeled (`printed.rs` reads them from the printed type and refuses text that does not read to its end; a fact it cannot read is never replaced by a guess).

- **Named boundary.** An interface or class declared under `node_modules` or in the TypeScript lib (`Date`, `Promise<T>`, `HTMLElement`), and an object type a dependency's alias names, stay `named` with their arguments. A function type is always expanded. The lib's utilities (`Partial`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`) are expanded: their result is the type. A dependency's union of literals is expanded, since its members are the values a control offers. React's `ReactNode`, `ElementType`, `CSSProperties` and `ReactElement` are recognized by where they are declared.
- **Caps.** Depth 5, 500 members at the top and 120 below it (a union, an intersection, a tuple's elements), and a budget of 100 properties at the top and 40 below it that counts only the members the project did not declare (inherited from a dependency or the lib, or with no declaration). A cut type is `truncated` with the limit (and, for a width, the total), which `degradedBy` reports. Every descent into the parts of a type (an object, union, intersection, array, tuple or template literal) passes one gate (`Converter::enter`) that checks, before anything is fetched, whether the type encloses itself or is too deep; the width is checked after it, where the type is known. A test has a prop for each cap.
- **Wide object types.** What the project declares is listed whole however wide: an interface of 150 own fields is never cut. Over the budget of members from outside the project, the rest stands as what it is named through, and the project's own members stay beside it. A utility wrapper (`Omit`, `Pick`, `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`) is kept as `named` with its arguments when what it applies to has a name of its own: a React DOM attribute type becomes `htmlAttributes` (recognized by the declaring file `/@types/react/` and the interface's name, with the element read from its type argument by the same table the structural path uses, `HTMLAnchorElement` is `a`; an element the table does not know is not guessed), and another dependency or lib type is a `named` layer. The checker keeps no `ComponentPropsWithoutRef`, only the `Omit<..., "ref">` it expands to, which is kept as written. Under the budget the wrapper is expanded (`Pick<ComponentProps<"button">, "disabled" | "type">` has two props). A class or interface of the project that extends such types (`interface BoxProps extends Omit<HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>, "color">`) is an intersection of its own fields and each base type (`getBaseTypes`), a base of the project seen through to its own bases; an instantiation of a generic one, as the type itself or as one base among others, states no bases in terms of its arguments, so the type is cut: its members from outside are `truncated` with their real count beside its own, and the other bases are not named in its place. A type that is not wrapped (`HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>` as a prop) is the `named` it always was.
- **React aliases flattened into a union.** The checker flattens `ReactNode | Fn` into the members of `ReactNode`, so a union that holds all of them (`ReactElement`, `ReactPortal` and an `Iterable` of `ReactNode`, found by declaration, with the primitives) is `reactNode` again beside the rest of its members. `ElementType` below the top of a prop arrives the same way and is wider than the budget: it is recognized (more than 100 of React's own tag names, a fixed table of `JSX.IntrinsicElements`, with `ComponentClass` and `FunctionComponent`) and kept as the terminal instead of cut, and only those tag names go into it: any other string literal the author wrote beside it (`ElementType | "custom-widget"`) stays a member of the union, as does a tag a project adds to `JSX.IntrinsicElements`; narrower, it is listed. `ReactElement`, `JSX.Element` and `ReactChild` stay collapsed to `reactNode` (ADR 0026).
- **Recursion** is a `recursive` marker named by the declaration (the alias or interface) with the instantiation's type arguments. Whether a type is one it is inside of is decided by its type handle, which is the instantiation: `Box<string>` inside `Box<Box<string>>` is another type from the one around it and is expanded, while `Tree<string>` inside `Tree<string>` is a back-reference; an alias of an array or tuple of itself (`type Loop = Loop[]`) ends at the first lap. A handle is only compared inside one conversion, never stored in an answer; type handles change with the order of queries, so a test asks last to first and compares bytes. The per-snapshot memo is keyed by the handle, the depth and the set of enclosing handles, so a hit gives what a miss would.
- **Union order.** The checker sorts a union's members by kind and value. Where the structural pass resolved the same union (in a parsed file, or a loaded dependency), the merge puts the members back in its order, which it read from the type node (`types/semantic/order.rs`). A union the structural pass left opaque keeps the checker's order, with no marker.
- **Debug stat.** With `RUST_LOG=caliper_docgen_semantic=debug`, each component logs its request count and milliseconds, and the session logs requests by method and memo hits.

### The checker's answer wins (ADR 0026, slice S4)

The checker stays an explicit opt-in (`--experimental-semantic-types`, `semanticTypes: 'on-demand'`); the default flips in S8. When it runs, its answer replaces the structural one prop by prop, at each surface:

- **CLI.** `extract --experimental-semantic-types` waits for the checker: every candidate component in one program and one snapshot, as in slice 1. `--semantic-timeout-ms` (default 10,000) bounds the checker's start and each request; past it the run takes the structural result with one `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` warning that says it timed out. It bounds a hang, not the run: on 938 Chakra and MUI wrappers (`~/Projects/caliper-fixtures/gate-large`) the whole answer takes 17 s with tsrs, its program 71 ms, and no request comes near the bound.
- **Addon and sessions.** Unchanged from ADR 0022: the structural answer first, the checker's within `semanticWaitMs` (default 150), a late answer for the next request. The premise that the checker is too slow for a first story still holds with tsrs: Chakra's `Button` (about 1,100 props) takes a median 562 ms through the Rust client, so it arrives on the next request (see [gate measurements](gate-measurements.md#first-answer-s4)).
- **A prop the checker could not read.** Where the checker's type of a prop holds an `opaque` part (an import or a name it did not resolve, a conditional type it left open, signatures it could not read) and the structural pass read the same prop's type in full, the prop keeps the structural type and its `degradedBy` also lists the checker's reasons: the checker did not confirm the type, so it is marked rather than silently trusted. One `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` `Info` diagnostic counts those props and names their components. A type the checker only cut at a limit (`truncated`) is still its answer, and so is an opaque checker type where the structural one is opaque too. On the 938 wrappers this applies to 60 props (Chakra's `cornerShape`, whose `CssProperties["cornerShape"]` the checker reads as an error type with the installed `csstype`, and `storageManager`, whose interface's signatures it could not read).
- **Gate.** The construct suite's checker lane holds `checker-expectations.json` against `expectations.json`: no row may rank below the structural path unless it lists an `improvement` reason (`apps/oracle/construct-suite/README.md`, "The checker lane").

## First answer (S4)

- **The gate.** S4: "Chakra first answer at most 150 ms through the Rust client", the addon's default `semanticWaitMs`, which decides whether a first story shows the checker's props or the structural ones.
- **How.** `gate_harness first-answer` (the third gate `just gate-measure` runs) opens, `--runs` times (default 5), a fresh lazy session configured as the addon configures it (dependencies loaded, nothing collapsed, the default `htmlAttributes`), starts the checker in the background as the addon does at creation, waits until that process is up and initialized, then times one `component("ChakraButton")`: the structural pass and the checker's program and conversion for that one component, through the same `OnDemand` the addon uses. It passes when every answer is the checker's and the median is at most `--budget-ms` (150).
- **Result (2026-11-09, `feat/checker-wins`, tsrs `0.23.0-ts7.1.0-beta`, 9 runs, a shared machine at load 13):** every answer was the checker's; median **562 ms** (557 to 575), of which the structural answer is 5 ms and the process start, already done before the request, 5 ms. **FAIL.**
- **Where the time goes.** One answer is about 4,400 requests to tsrs, one at a time: the props of `ButtonProps` are mostly Chakra's style props, each a distinct instantiated union (1,800 `getTypesOfType`, 1,250 `getTypeArguments`, 600 `typeToString`, 560 `batchRequests`, and 43 ms for the snapshot). tsrs answers a request in about 70 µs. Three changes were tried and not kept: converting 16 props at once (360 to 390 ms, but it changes which type handle first asks about a symbol, so the replay fixtures no longer match and would need recording again), batching the requests a level of the walk will make (no faster: tsrs's time per answer, not the round trip, is the cost) and one documentation batch per component (5%). What would meet 150 ms is fewer requests per component, for example expanding a dependency's instantiated aliases on demand; that is converter work beyond S4.
- **Verdict: FAIL**, so ADR 0022's premise stands with tsrs: a story shows the structural props first and the checker's from the next request on.
